title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 37
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Flattening a Sphere
passages.text:
A. Every flat map of the world is wrong, and this is a mathematical certainty rather than a criticism of mapmakers. A curved surface cannot be represented on a plane without distorting something — area, shape, distance or direction — and it can be proved that no projection preserves all of them. The question is never which map is accurate but which distortion the map's purpose can afford.

B. The projection that dominates general use was designed for a task nobody now uses it for. It was constructed so that a line of constant compass bearing appears as a straight line, which is precisely what a navigator steering by compass requires and is of no use whatever to a reader looking at a wall map. Its cost is that area inflates towards the poles, so high-latitude landmasses appear enormously larger than equatorial ones.

C. The political criticism of that inflation is correct in substance and often confused in explanation. The distortion does systematically enlarge some regions relative to others, and generations of readers have absorbed a false sense of relative size. The projection was not, however, devised for that purpose; it was devised for navigation, and its persistence owes more to institutional inertia and to its convenience for square screens than to intent.

D. The alternatives each buy their virtue with a specific loss. Projections that preserve area distort shape, sometimes severely, so continents appear stretched or sheared; compromise projections distort everything slightly and nothing badly, which suits an atlas and suits no calculation; and projections centred on a particular region serve that region well and the rest poorly. There is no default that is correct, only defaults appropriate to purposes.

E. What digital mapping changed was the scale at which the problem appears rather than the problem itself. At the scale of a street or a city, the curvature is negligible and any projection will do; the distortions that matter are visible only at continental scale, which is exactly the scale at which people now most often see maps as a background to something else. The projection is chosen by the software and noticed by nobody.

F. The deeper point is about all representation rather than about maps. A map is useful because it discards almost everything, and its selection of what to keep encodes a purpose that the reader is rarely told. Boundaries shown or omitted, names in which language, roads or footpaths emphasised — these are decisions, and the appearance of neutrality that a printed map carries is the most misleading thing about it.

passages.title: Light Made by Animals
passages.text:
Most of the animal kingdom's light is made in the sea, and the proportion of deep-sea species capable of producing it is high enough that light-making should be considered the norm rather than the curiosity. The chemistry is broadly similar wherever it appears: a molecule is oxidised in the presence of an enzyme, releasing energy as light rather than as heat, and the efficiency is extraordinary — almost none of the energy is wasted warming the animal.

The distribution of the ability across the tree of life is the puzzle. It appears in bacteria, fungi, insects, molluscs, crustaceans and fish, in groups too distantly related for a common origin, which means it evolved independently many times over. A capability that arises repeatedly is usually one that is easy to arrive at and useful in many situations, and both appear to be true here.

The functions divide into a few categories that account for most cases. Light attracts prey, as in the lure of the anglerfish; it deters predators, either by startling them or by illuminating them for something larger; it communicates, particularly for mating, where species-specific flash patterns function as a signal that cannot be misread; and in mid-water it conceals, which is the least obvious use and possibly the most common.

Concealment by light is worth explaining because it inverts the expected logic. In open water at moderate depth, an animal seen from below appears as a dark silhouette against faint light from the surface, and the way to disappear is not to be dark but to emit light downwards matching the background. Many mid-water animals carry light organs on their undersides, adjust their output to the ambient light, and become invisible from beneath by glowing.

A large share of the light is not made by the animal at all. Many fish and squid house colonies of luminous bacteria in specialised organs, feeding them and controlling their output with shutters and reflectors, which is a division of labour rather than a possession of the ability. The relationship is specific enough that some hosts acquire their bacteria from seawater after hatching and cannot produce light until they do.

The applied consequences have been substantial and are rarely connected to their origin. The proteins responsible, isolated from a jellyfish, became a standard laboratory tool for making the activity of genes visible inside living cells, which transformed a great deal of biological research. The work began as curiosity about why an animal glows, and the eventual application could not have been specified in advance by anyone.

passages.title: What the Fare Is For
passages.text:
A public transport fare is not principally a price and treating it as one produces most of the confusion in the argument about it. The cost of carrying one additional passenger on a service already running is close to nothing, so a fare set to recover that cost would be near zero; the fare exists to contribute to fixed costs and to manage demand, and those two purposes conflict at the busiest times.

Cost recovery varies enormously and rarely covers the service. Fares typically fund between a quarter and three-quarters of operating cost depending on the city, and almost never the capital cost of the infrastructure, which is funded from taxation or borrowing. This is not a failure of efficiency; it follows from a service that must run at low-demand times to be useful at high-demand ones, and from the benefits it produces for people who never board.

Those external benefits are the strongest part of the case and the hardest to put in a budget. A functioning transit system reduces road congestion for drivers, permits higher-density development, lowers emissions per journey, and gives access to employment to people who cannot drive. None of these accrues to the operator, all are real, and their value has been estimated repeatedly at figures well above the subsidy — which is an argument for public funding rather than for a higher fare.

Free travel is the proposal that most divides the evidence from the enthusiasm. Where it has been implemented, ridership rises, and the increase comes substantially from people who previously walked or cycled rather than from drivers; the switch from cars is smaller than expected because the barrier to driving is rarely the fare. Removing fare revenue also removes the funding for the frequency and reliability that actually attract drivers, which is why several systems have concluded that better service at a moderate fare beats a free but thinner one.

Peak pricing follows from the cost structure and is politically difficult for a specific reason. Capacity is built for the peak, so peak journeys impose the cost that determines the system's size, and charging more at those times is economically correct. It also charges most to people whose hours are fixed by their employer and least to those who can travel when they choose, which reverses the usual relationship between flexibility and income.

The distributional question is where the argument should sit and rarely does. Who pays and who benefits depends on where the routes go, who lives near them, and which trips the timetable serves — a network built around commuting into a centre serves a different population from one built around movement between districts. That choice does more to determine who gains than any fare policy applied on top of it.
